nodes.name: ʻŌhiʻa lehua
nodes.desc: A native tree whose flowers give nectar to honeycreepers. It grows in many Hawaiian forests and is a foundation of the native forest.

nodes.name: Māmane
nodes.desc: A native subalpine tree whose flowers are nectar for ʻamakihi and ʻiʻiwi. It grows on the high slopes of Hawaiian volcanoes.

nodes.name: Haleakalā silversword
nodes.desc: A silver-leaved plant found only on Haleakalā, above about 2,100 m. It is federally threatened, and introduced hoofed animals are a major reason it declined.

nodes.name: ʻŌhelo
nodes.desc: A native shrub of volcanic slopes with edible red or yellow berries that birds such as the nēnē eat.

nodes.name: Pūkiawe
nodes.desc: A native shrub of forests, bogs and alpine shrubland. Nēnē and other birds eat its berries and spread the seeds.

nodes.name: Moths
nodes.desc: Moths are prey for the native bat and for forest birds, and the most common insects in ʻapapane stomachs in one study. Caterpillars feed on forest plants.

nodes.name: Nēnē (Hawaiian goose)
nodes.desc: An endangered goose that eats leaves, seeds and fruit of grasses and shrubs. It died out in the park and was reintroduced in 1962.

nodes.name: Feral goat
nodes.desc: An introduced browser. Feral goats generally overgraze native plants and cause erosion, and the park lists feral hoofed animals as damaging to native vegetation.

nodes.name: Feral pig
nodes.desc: An introduced rooting omnivore. Wikipedia says wallows of feral pigs breed mosquito larvae, which spread avian malaria to native birds.

nodes.name: Black rat
nodes.desc: An introduced rodent that eats fruit, seeds and insects. It is prey for cats, mongooses and owls.

nodes.name: Japanese white-eye
nodes.desc: A very common introduced songbird that eats berries, nectar and insects. It is prey for cats and owls.

nodes.name: Hawaiʻi ʻamakihi
nodes.desc: A native honeycreeper that drinks nectar from ʻōhiʻa and māmane flowers and hunts insects and spiders. It is among the most recorded birds near the park.

nodes.name: ʻApapane
nodes.desc: A native honeycreeper that drinks ʻōhiʻa nectar and pollinates it. It also takes insects and spiders, mostly moths and butterflies in one study.

nodes.name: ʻIʻiwi
nodes.desc: A native honeycreeper that drinks nectar from lobelias and ʻōhiʻa and eats small arthropods. Avian malaria is the main driver of its decline.

nodes.name: ʻŌpeʻapeʻa (Hawaiian hoary bat)
nodes.desc: The native land mammal. It is a generalist insect eater that mainly takes moths and beetles, in open areas and in forest.

nodes.name: Small Indian mongoose
nodes.desc: An introduced predator and the most recorded mammal near the park. It eats rodents, insects, birds and eggs and was named as a predator of nēnē.

nodes.name: Feral cat
nodes.desc: An introduced top predator. GloBI records list it eating many birds, rats and mice. Wikipedia names feral cats among the predators that nearly wiped out the nēnē.

nodes.name: Pueo (short-eared owl)
nodes.desc: A hunting owl of open country. GloBI records list it eating rodents and small birds near the park.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Strong sun at high elevation drives plant growth, while the alpine summit is cold and dry.

nodes.name: Rainfall
nodes.desc: Wet windward forests get heavy rain, while the summit is dry. Rain also supports the mosquitoes that spread avian malaria.

nodes.name: Volcanic soil
nodes.desc: Young lava and ash soils hold the nutrients the plants draw on, and are returned by decomposers.

nodes.name: Cool upland air
nodes.desc: Cooler air at high elevation keeps mosquitoes and avian malaria down, so it is a refuge for native forest birds.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Break down dead leaves, wood and animals and return nutrients to the volcanic soil.
